evidence_quotes.quote: Este artigo tem por objetivos analisar a noção da água com bem comum construída por populações rurais, investigar as bases em que essa concepção se fundamenta e, por fim, avaliar os impactos que a centralização da gestão da água causa sobre as culturas locais na gestão de recursos hídricos.

Esse estudo é fruto de pesquisa realizada entre 2002 e 2009 em comunidades rurais de três regiões de Minas Gerais: os vales do rio São Francisco, do rio Jequitinhonha e a Serra da Mantiqueira. Essa escolha buscou diversidade de ambientes e de oferta de água (abundância ou escassez). Ao total foram pesquisadas dezoito localidades.

Foram usados dois roteiros de pesquisa: um para observação do ambiente, partilha da terra e sistemas de lavouras; outro para entrevista, bastante aberto, buscava informações sobre família, comunidade, terra e água.

Esta concepção norteia uma ética que baliza códigos de uso familiares e comunitários. A ética, aliada ao conhecimento do recurso, fundamenta as categorias refinadas de classificação da qualidade da água estabelecidas pelas várias comunidades.
Por um lado, o Instituto Estadual de Florestas impunha a conservação de mananciais por meio da lei, da polícia florestal e das multas, apesar de constantemente desafiados pelas famílias.
No Brasil qual espaço político e cultural a Lei das Águas – participativa, mas excludente – e o mercado – que concebe água como bem econômico – deixarão para a pequena regulação comunitária?

criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1 (and matches Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). The paper examines rural farming communities' cultural conceptions, folk classifications, and customary sharing of natural water sources (springs/nascentes, streams/córregos, and rivers/rios) as common-pool natural resources (gestão de recursos hídricos), with no piped network, water utility, community water supply infrastructure, or sanitation service examined.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2 ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper examines customary community governance norms (normas costumeiras, servidões comunitárias) for natural water sources, mentions state forestry enforcement of springhead conservation (Instituto Estadual de Florestas police and fines), and offers a one-paragraph concluding critique of Brazil's federal Water Law (Lei das Águas); however, all of these concern natural water-resource/watershed governance rather than water or sanitation service access. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, Criterion 2 is clearly 'no': the paper does not examine any rule-type mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements for service connection, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, service enforcement/disconnection, or utility ownership/regulatory structure), and the Lei das Águas appears only as unanalysed macro-governance background in the final section.
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies Criterion 3: reports qualitative empirical fieldwork conducted between 2002 and 2009 across 18 rural communities in three regions of Minas Gerais using observation guides, open-ended interviews with farming families, and community meetings.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: does not report household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, continuity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes. Instead, it reports folk classifications of raw water quality (água viva vs. água morta; águas pequenas vs. águas grandes), moral/religious reciprocity norms and sanctions, springhead revegetation (26 springs fenced), and perceived river depletion and agricultural land-use restrictions (prejudicou as roças).
criterion_notes.c5: Although the qualitative multi-site design and study population/unit of analysis (18 rural communities/bairros rurais and farming families in Minas Gerais) are identifiable, no water or sanitation service-access exposure or service-access outcome can be identified, and Quadro 1 (Amostra pesquisada) and Quadro 2 are omitted/blank in the extracted article text.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Portuguese, which is eligible without translation under Criterion 9.

study_design: Qualitative multi-site field study (ethnographic / rural-sociological study using environmental observation, open-ended family interviews, and community meetings)
population_and_sample: 18 rural communities (comunidades or bairros rurais as unit of analysis) and farming families (famílias de lavradores) across three regions of Minas Gerais, Brazil (São Francisco valley, Jequitinhonha valley, and Serra da Mantiqueira), studied between 2002 and 2009 (Quadro 1 sample table blank in PDF text)
exposure: Customary peasant moral norms and community common-pool water resource management (normas costumeiras / ética da água como bem comum), alongside environmental springhead conservation enforcement (Instituto Estadual de Florestas fines and NGO springhead fencing) and macro-level commentary on Brazil's Water Law (Lei das Águas)
outcome: Folk classifications of raw water quality (água viva/corrente vs. água morta/parada; águas pequenas vs. águas grandes), customary sharing practices and moral/divine sanctions around natural springs and streams, springhead revegetation (26 springs), and perceived river depletion and agricultural plot restrictions from springhead conservation (no water or sanitation service access outcome reported)
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic — natural water-resources and rural common-pool moral economy study unrelated to household or community water or sanitation service access, per Exclusion Criterion 7). Based on qualitative fieldwork in 18 rural communities in Minas Gerais, Brazil, the article analyzes peasant cultural conceptions of natural water (springs, streams, rivers) as a divine gift and common good, folk water-quality classifications, and watershed conservation tensions (upstream irrigation diversions, forestry fines restricting wetland farming, and community springhead fencing). It examines no water supply or sanitation service, reports no service-access outcome, and analyzes no legal or administrative rule-type mechanism governing service access (referencing Brazil's Lei das Águas only as unanalysed macro-governance background in the closing section). Under both the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading and the plain wording, the study is excluded because it concerns common-pool natural water resource ethics and watershed conservation rather than water or sanitation service access.
